exampleAnswers.title: Identifying Elements Belonging to an Equivalence Class

question.text:
Consider the equivalence relation $\sim$ on $\mathbb{R},$ defined by $x \sim y$ if $x^4 = y^4.$ Which of the following are in the equivalence class $[-1]?$

  1. $1$
  2. $4$
  3. $-1$
question.explanation:
The equivalence class $[-1]$ consists of the elements that are equivalent to $-1$ under the given equivalence relation. So, we have

\begin{align*} [-1] &= \{ x \in \mathbb{R} \: | \: x \sim -1 \} \\[5pt] &= \{ x \in \mathbb{R} \: | \: x^4 = (-1)^4 \} \\[5pt] &= \{ x \in \mathbb{R} \: | \: x^4-1 = 0 \} \\[5pt] &= \{ x \in \mathbb{R} \: | \:(x^2+1) (x^2-1 )= 0 \} \\[5pt] &= \{ x \in \mathbb{R} \: | \: x^2-1 = 0 \} \\[5pt] &= \{ x \in \mathbb{R} \: | \: x^2 = 1 \} \\[5pt] &= \{ -1, 1 \}. \end{align*}

We see that $-1$ and $1$ are in $[-1],$ while $4$ is not.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

example.title: Identifying Elements Belonging to an Equivalence Class

question.text:
Consider the equivalence relation $\sim$ on $\mathbb{R},$ defined by $x \sim y$ if $x^3 = y^3.$ Which of the following are in the equivalence class $[8]?$

  1. $-2$
  2. $2$
  3. $8$
question.explanation:
The equivalence class $[8]$ consists of the elements that are equivalent to $8$ under the given equivalence relation. So, we have

\begin{align*} [8] &= \{ x \in \mathbb{R} \: | \: x \sim 8 \} \\[3pt] &= \{ x \in \mathbb{R} \: | \: x^3 = 8^3 \} \\[3pt] &= \{ x \in \mathbb{R} \: | \: x = 8 \} \\[3pt] &= \{ 8 \}. \end{align*}

We see that $8$ is in $[8],$ while $-2$ and $2$ are not.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only".

example.title: Identifying Elements Belonging to an Equivalence Class

question.text:
Consider the equivalence relation $\sim$ on $\mathbb{R},$ defined by $x \sim y$ if $\sin x = \sin y.$ Which of the following are in the equivalence class $[-\pi]?$

  1. $0$
  2. $-\dfrac{\pi}{2}$
  3. $\pi$
question.explanation:
The equivalence class $[-\pi]$ consists of the elements that are equivalent to $-\pi$ under the given equivalence relation. So, we have

\begin{align*} [-\pi] &= \{ x \in \mathbb{R} \: | \: x \sim -\pi \} \\[5pt] &= \{ x \in \mathbb{R} \: | \: \sin x = \sin (-\pi) \} \\[5pt] &= \{ x \in \mathbb{R} \: | \: \sin x = 0 \} \\[5pt] &= \{ \ldots, -2\pi, -\pi, 0, \pi, 2\pi, \ldots \}. \end{align*}

We see that $0$ and $\pi$ are in $[-\pi],$ while $-\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ is not.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

example.title: Identifying Elements Belonging to an Equivalence Class

question.text:
Consider the equivalence relation $\sim$ on $\mathbb{Z},$ defined by $x \sim y$ if $7 \,|\, (x-y).$ Which of the following are in the equivalence class $[5]?$

  1. $12$
  2. $-4$
  3. $-2$
question.explanation:
The equivalence class $[5]$ consists of the elements that are equivalent to $5$ under the given equivalence relation. So, we have

\begin{align*} [5] &= \{ x \in \mathbb{Z} \: : \: x \sim 5 \} \\[5pt] &= \{ x \in \mathbb{Z} \: : \: 7 \,|\, (x-5) \} \\[5pt] &= \{ x \in \mathbb{Z} \: : \: x = 5+7k, k\in\mathbb Z\} \\[5pt] &= \{ \ldots, -9, -2, 5, 12, 19, \ldots \}. \end{align*}

We see that $12$ and $-2$ are in $[5],$ while $-4$ is not.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

example.title: Identifying Elements Belonging to an Equivalence Class

question.text:
Consider the equivalence relation $\sim$ on $\mathbb{R},$ defined by $x \sim y$ if $\sqrt[3]{x} = \sqrt[3]{y}.$ Which of the following are in the equivalence class $[-8]?$

  1. $-8$
  2. $8$
  3. $2$
question.explanation:
The equivalence class $[-8]$ consists of the elements that are equivalent to $-8$ under the given equivalence relation. So, we have

\begin{align*} [-8] &= \{ x \in \mathbb{R} \: | \: x \sim -8 \} \\[3pt] &= \{ x \in \mathbb{R} \: | \: \sqrt[3]{x} = \sqrt[3]{-8} \} \\[3pt] &= \{ x \in \mathbb{R} \: | \: \sqrt[3]{x} = -2 \} \\[3pt] &= \{ -8 \}. \end{align*}

We see that $-8$ is in $[-8],$ while $8$ and $2$ are not.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only".

exampleAnswers.title: Identifying Equivalence Classes Containing a Given Element

question.text:
Consider the equivalence relation $\sim$ on $\mathbb{R},$ defined by $x \sim y$ if $\sin x = \sin y.$ Which of the following equivalence classes contain the element ${4\pi}?$

  1. $[-\pi]$
  2. $\left[\dfrac{\pi}2\right]$
  3. $[3\pi]$
question.explanation:
We have $4\pi \in [x]$ if $4\pi\sim x .$ Using the definition of the given equivalence relation, we require

\begin{align*} \sin (4\pi ) & = \sin x\\[3pt] 0 &= \sin x \\[3pt] \sin x &= 0 \end{align*}

Let's now consider each of the given equivalence classes.

  • $4\pi \in [-\pi]$ because $\sin(-\pi) =0 \quad \color{green}\checkmark$

  • $4\pi \not\in \left[\dfrac{\pi}2\right]$ because $\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}2\right) = 1 \neq 0 \quad \color{red}\times$

  • $4\pi \in [3\pi]$ because $\sin(3\pi) =0 \quad \color{green}\checkmark$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

example.title: Identifying Equivalence Classes Containing a Given Element

question.text:
Consider the equivalence relation $\sim$ on $\mathbb{R},$ defined by $x \sim y$ if $\sqrt[3]{x} = \sqrt[3]{y}.$ Which of the following equivalence classes contain the element $64?$

  1. $[64]$
  2. $[-64]$
  3. $[8]$
question.explanation:
We have $64 \in [x]$ if $64 \sim x.$ Using the definition of the given equivalence relation, we require

\begin{align*} \sqrt[3]{64} &= \sqrt[3]{x} \\[3pt] 4 &= \sqrt[3]{x} \\[3pt] \sqrt[3]{x} &= 4. \end{align*}

Let's now consider each of the given equivalence classes.

  • $64 \in [64]$ because $\sqrt[3]{64} = 4 \quad \color{green}\checkmark$

  • $64 \not\in [-64]$ because $\sqrt[3]{-64} = -4\neq 4 \quad \color{red}\times$

  • $64 \not\in [8]$ because $\sqrt[3]{8} = 2 \neq 4 \quad \color{red}\times$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only".

example.title: Identifying Equivalence Classes Containing a Given Element

question.text:
Consider the equivalence relation $\sim$ on $\mathbb{R},$ defined by $x \sim y$ if $\sin \pi x = \sin\pi y.$ Which of the following equivalence classes contain the element $-\dfrac{1}2?$

  1. $[0]$
  2. $\left[\dfrac{1}2\right]$
  3. $\left[\dfrac{3}2\right]$
question.explanation:
We have $-\dfrac12\in [x]$ if $-\dfrac12\sim x .$ Using the definition of the given equivalence relation, we require

\begin{align*} \sin \left(\pi\cdot\left(-\dfrac12\right)\right) & = \sin \pi x\\[3pt] -\sin \left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) & = \sin \pi x\\[3pt] -1 &= \sin \pi x \\[3pt] \sin \pi x &= -1 \end{align*}

Let's now consider each of the given equivalence classes.

  • $-\dfrac{1}2 \not\in \left[0\right]$ because $\sin\left(\pi\cdot 0\right) = 0 \neq -1 \quad \color{red}\times$

  • $-\dfrac{1}2\not\in\left[\dfrac{1}2\right]$ because $\sin\left(\pi\cdot \dfrac{1}{2}\right) =1 \neq -1 \quad \color{red}\times$

  • $-\dfrac{1}2 \in\left[\dfrac{3}2\right]$ because $\sin\left(\pi\cdot \dfrac{3}{2}\right) =-1 \quad \color{green}\checkmark$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

example.title: Identifying Equivalence Classes Containing a Given Element

question.text:
Consider the equivalence relation $\sim$ on $\mathbb{Z},$ defined by $x \sim y$ if $7 \,|\, (x-y).$ Which of the following equivalence classes contain the element $2?$

  1. $[1]$
  2. $[0]$
  3. $[9]$
question.explanation:
We have $2 \in [x]$ if $2 \sim x.$ Using the definition of the given equivalence relation, we require

\begin{align*} 7 \,|\, (2-x). \end{align*}

Let's now consider each of the given equivalence classes.

  • $2 \not\in [1]$ because $7 \not\mid (2-1) \quad \color{red}\times$

  • $2 \not\in [0]$ because $7 \not\mid (2-0) \quad \color{red}\times$

  • $2 \in [9]$ because $7 \,|\, (2-9) \quad \color{green}\checkmark$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

example.title: Identifying Equivalence Classes Containing a Given Element

question.text:
Consider the equivalence relation $\sim$ on $\mathbb{Z},$ defined by $x \sim y$ if $5 \,|\, (x-y).$ Which of the following equivalence classes contain the element $-4?$

  1. $[-14]$
  2. $[11]$
  3. $[14]$
question.explanation:
We have $-4 \in [x]$ if $-4 \sim x.$ Using the definition of the given equivalence relation, we require

\begin{align*} 5 \,|\, (-4-x). \end{align*}

Let's now consider each of the given equivalence classes.

  • $-4 \in [-14]$ because $5 \,|\, (-4+14) \quad \color{green}\checkmark$

  • $-4 \in [11]$ because $5 \,|\, (-4-11) \quad \color{green}\checkmark$

  • $-4 \not\in [14]$ because $5 \not\mid (-4-14) \quad \color{red}\times$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only".

example.title: Identifying Equivalence Classes Containing a Given Element

question.text: Consider the equivalence relation $\sim$ on the set $A = \{0, 1, 2, \ldots, 9\},$ defined by $a \sim b$ if $2 \mid (b-a).$ How many distinct equivalence classes does $\sim$ partition $A$ into?
question.explanation:
The equivalence classes of $\sim$ partition $A,$ meaning that any element $a \in A$ belongs to exactly one distinct equivalence class.

So, we compute equivalence classes until all the elements of $A$ have been placed into an equivalence class.

\[ \begin{align*} [0] &= \{ a \in A \: : \: a \sim 0 \} \\[3pt] &= \{ a \in A \: : \: 2\ \mid (a-0)\} \\[3pt] &= \{ a \in A \: : \: 2 \mid a\} \\[3pt] &= \{ 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 \} \\ \\ [1] &= \{ a \in A \: : \: a \sim 1 \} \\[3pt] &= \{ a \in A \: : \: 2 \mid (a-1)\} \\[3pt] &= \{ 1, 3, 5, 7,9\} \\ \\ \end{align*} \]

All of the elements of $A$ have been placed into an equivalence class, so we are done.

We have $2$ distinct equivalence classes:

\[ [0] = \{ 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 \} , \quad [1] = \{ 1, 3, 5, 7,9 \}. \]

Notice that the equivalence classes form a partition of $A,$ as expected.

question.text: Consider the equivalence relation $\sim$ on the set $A = \{1, 2,3, 4\},$ defined by \[ \left\{ {\left( {1,1} \right),\left( {2,2} \right),\left( {3,3} \right),\left( {3,4} \right),\left( {4,3} \right), \left( {4,4} \right)} \right\}. \] How many distinct equivalence classes does $\sim$ partition $A$ into?
question.explanation:
The equivalence classes of $\sim$ partition $A,$ meaning that any element $a \in A$ belongs to exactly one distinct equivalence class.

So, we compute equivalence classes until all the elements of $A$ have been placed into an equivalence class.

\[ \begin{align*} [1] &= \{ a \in A \mid a \sim 1 \} \\[3pt] &= \{ 1\} \end{align*} \] \[ \begin{align*} [2] &= \{ a \in A \mid a \sim 2 \} \\[3pt] &= \{ 2\} \end{align*} \] \[ \begin{align*} [3] &= \{ a \in A \mid a \sim 3 \} \\[3pt] &= \{ 3,4\} \end{align*} \] We skip $[ 4 ]$ since we already know that $ 4 \in [3]$

All of the elements of $A$ have been placed into an equivalence class, so we are done.

We have $3$ distinct equivalence classes:

\[ [1] = \{ 1 \}, \quad [2] = \{ 2 \}, \quad [3] = \{ 3,4 \}. \]

Notice that the equivalence classes form a partition of $A,$ as expected.

question.text: Consider the equivalence relation $\sim$ on the set $A = \{0, 1, 2, \ldots, 9\},$ defined by $a \sim b$ if $7 \mid (b-a).$ How many distinct equivalence classes does $\sim$ partition $A$ into?
question.explanation:
The equivalence classes of $\sim$ partition $A,$ meaning that any element $a \in A$ belongs to exactly one distinct equivalence class.

So, we compute equivalence classes until all the elements of $A$ have been placed into an equivalence class.

\[ \begin{align*} [0] &= \{ a \in A \: : \: a \sim 0 \} \\[3pt] &= \{ a \in A \: : \: 7 \mid (a-0)\} \\[3pt] &= \{ a \in A \: : \: 7 \mid a\} \\[3pt] &= \{ 0, 7 \} \\ \\ [1] &= \{ a \in A \: : \: a \sim 1 \} \\[3pt] &= \{ a \in A \: : \: 7 \mid (a-1)\} \\[3pt] &= \{ 1, 8 \} \\ \\ [2] &= \{ a \in A \: : \: a \sim 2 \} \\[3pt] &= \{ a \in A \: : \: 7 \mid (a-2)\} \\[3pt] &= \{ 2, 9\} \\ \\ [3] &= \{ a \in A \: : \: a \sim 3 \} \\[3pt] &= \{ a \in A \: : \: 7 \mid (a-3)\} \\[3pt] &= \{ 3\} \\ \\ [4] &= \{ a \in A \: : \: a \sim 4 \} \\[3pt] &= \{ a \in A \: : \: 7 \mid (a-4)\} \\[3pt] &= \{4\} \\ \\ [5] &= \{ a \in A \: : \: a \sim 5 \} \\[3pt] &= \{ a \in A \: : \: 7 \mid (a-5)\} \\[3pt] &= \{5\} \\ \\ [6] &= \{ a \in A \: : \: a \sim 6\} \\[3pt] &= \{ a \in A \: : \: 7 \mid (a-6)\} \\[3pt] &= \{6\} \\ \\ \end{align*} \]

All of the elements of $A$ have been placed into an equivalence class, so we are done.

We have $7$ distinct equivalence classes:

\[ [0] = \{ 0, 7 \} , \quad [1] = \{ 1, 8 \}, \quad [2] = \{ 2,9 \}, \quad [3] = \{ 3 \}\quad [4] = \{ 4 \},\quad [5] = \{ 5 \},\quad [6] = \{ 6 \}. \]

Notice that the equivalence classes form a partition of $A,$ as expected.

The equivalence classes of $\sim$ partition $A,$ meaning that any element $a \in A$ belongs to exactly one distinct equivalence class.

So, we compute equivalence classes until all the elements of $A$ have been placed into an equivalence class.

\[ \begin{align*} [0] &= \{ a \in A \mid a \sim 0 \} \\[3pt] &= \{ 0\} \end{align*} \] \[ \begin{align*} [1] &= \{ a \in A \mid a \sim 1 \} \\[3pt] &= \{ 1, 4\} \end{align*} \] \[ \begin{align*} [2] &= \{ a \in A \mid a \sim 2 \} \\[3pt] &= \{ 2\} \end{align*} \] \[ \begin{align*} [3] &= \{ a \in A \mid a \sim 3 \} \\[3pt] &= \{ 3\} \end{align*} \] We skip $[ 4 ] $ since we already know that $ 4 \in [1]$

question.text: Consider the equivalence relation $\sim$ on the set $A = \{0, 1, 2, \ldots, 9\},$ defined by $a \sim b$ if $\cos \left( \dfrac{\pi a}{2}\right)= \cos \left( \dfrac{\pi b}{2}\right).$ How many distinct equivalence classes does $\sim$ partition $A$ into?
question.explanation:
The equivalence classes of $\sim$ partition $A,$ meaning that any element $a \in A$ belongs to exactly one distinct equivalence class.

So, we compute equivalence classes until all the elements of $A$ have been placed into an equivalence class.

\[ \begin{align*} [0] &= \{ a \in A \mid a \sim 0 \} \\[3pt] &= \left\{ a \in A \mid \cos \left( \dfrac{\pi a}{2}\right)= \cos\left( \dfrac{\pi \cdot 0}{2}\right) \right\} \\[3pt] &= \left\{ a \in A \mid \cos \left( \dfrac{\pi a}{2}\right) = \cos \left( 0 \right) \right\} \\[3pt] &= \left\{ a \in A \mid \cos \left( \dfrac{\pi a}{2}\right) = 1 \right\} \\[3pt] &= \{ 0, 4, 8 \} \\ \\ [1] &= \left\{ a \in A \mid a \sim 1 \right\} \\[3pt] &= \left\{ a \in A \mid \cos \left( \dfrac{\pi a}{2}\right)= \cos\left( \dfrac{\pi \cdot 1}{2}\right) \right\} \\[3pt] &= \left\{ a \in A \mid \cos \left( \dfrac{\pi a}{2}\right) = \cos \left( \dfrac{\pi}2 \right) \right\} \\[3pt] &= \left\{ a \in A \mid \cos \left( \dfrac{\pi a}{2}\right) = 0 \right\} \\[3pt] &= \{ 1, 3, 5,7,9 \} \\ \\ [2] &= \{ a \in A \mid a \sim 2 \} \\[3pt] &= \left\{ a \in A \mid \cos \left( \dfrac{\pi a}{2}\right) = \cos \left( \dfrac{\pi \cdot 2}{2}\right) \right\} \\[3pt] &= \left\{ a \in A \mid \cos \left( \dfrac{\pi a}{2}\right) = \cos \left( \pi \right) \right\} \\[3pt] &= \left\{ a \in A \mid \cos \left( \dfrac{\pi a}{2}\right) = -1 \right\} \\[3pt] &= \{ 2, 6 \} \end{align*} \]

All of the elements of $A$ have been placed into an equivalence class, so we are done.

We have $3$ distinct equivalence classes:

\[ [0] = \{ 0, 4, 8 \} , \quad [1] = \{ 1,3, 5, 7,9 \}, \quad [2] = \{ 2, 6 \}. \]
